    Analog is a traditional FPV video system focused on long range & reliablity:

    Welcome to the wonderful world of antennas, its language & culture; to the aperture family (effective, reflective & scattering), the lobe family (main, side, back, & grating); to beam widths, directivity, dielectric conductivity & gain. Antennas are three-dimensional & live in a world of beam area, steradians, square degrees, & solid angle. Antennas have impedances (self & mutual). They couple to all of space & have a temperature measured in kelvins.

    An antenna is an array of conductors (elements), electrically connected to the receiver or transmitter. Antennas can be designed to transmit and receive radio waves in all horizontal directions equally (omnidirectional antennas), or preferentially in a particular direction (directional, or high-gain, or “beam” antennas).

    Antennas have polarizations: linear, elliptical, & circular.

    Ignore elliptical as this isn't used for our purposes i.e. large axial ratios. Some do actually exhibit elliptical polarization due to imperfections or environmental effects.

    Don't stomp on others channels when flying with companions: VTX table

    Note: some frequencies that isn't a highlighter hue are forbidden to transmit without prior legal body approval such as Lowband & specific channels. These are used by important entities such as Fire & Rescue or Military/Police. Bands for 915mHz, 1.3Ghz, 2.4Ghz & 3.3Ghz aren't shown for these reasons. Another is a narrow choice of open channels to choose from.

      FAQ

      What is analog?

      Analog is a one-way broadcast FPV system comprised of a modified D1/960H ColorVideoBlackingSync composite picture @ 60/50 interlaced fields per second.

      Figure 2. NTSC Composite Video Signal

      This format meshes image information—such as brightness (luminance), color (chrominance), & synchronization, into a single signal transmitted over one channel on 4:3/16:9 aspect ratio.

      Why do most goggles have two antennas equipped & how do they receive video?

    • Generic diversity switching: hops to either antenna that has better signal health which is called RSSI based on the module voltage.
    • Frame combining & sync reconstruction: fancy words for blending two analog fields together & sending a camera timing pulse when the feed becomes imperfect.

      • What is PIT mode?

      PITMode is a mode where the video transmitter only runs on incredibly low output power first introduced in the TBS Unify. This prevents interference with others at events while still allowing a minimum of visibility for emergency last-minute setting changes. With the TBS UNIFY PRO32 line, Pit Mode has been slightly modified in behavior. The main button on the video transmitter is used to toggle the PITMode flag at power-up, and SmartAudio / CRSF can modify this flag as well. Smart Audio can also enter pit mode during runtime using the power setting 0mW, which will not modify the flag (the VTX will never power up at the 0mW power setting). To leave PITMode during operation, simply set your desired power setting using Smart Audio, CRSF, or the button menu.

      What are the differences between CCD/DPS/CMOS?

      Charge-Coupled Device:

    • global shutter
    • maximum 650TVL
    • nearly immediate image when built properly
    • prone to smearing
    • homogeneous performance between brands excluding TBS zerozero
    • swift dark to bright environment transitions
    • best contrast

      • Digital-Pixel System: this CMOS unique to Pixim allows each pixel grid having their own analog-to-digital converter almost like how CCD shutters can/ maximum 690HTVL

      Fascinating technology, Sony bought Pixim not long after. Last available in "compact" form factor is the TBS 69.

      Never to used again.

      Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor:

    • rolling shutter
    • maximum 1800TVL
    • prone to shimmer
    • delayed conversion from the sensor to CVBS downstream
    • backlight-illuminated starlight sensors able to be flown after dusk

      • M12 large pitch lens are rarer to get

      What is DVR?

      DVR is a abbreviation of DigitalVideoRecorder. Always record DVR.

      What do the camera sizes mean?

    • Pico — 10x10mm 0.25"↔1/3" image sensor [whoop]
    • Nano — 14x14mm 1/3"↔1/2" image sensor [racing/most universal]
    • Micro — 19x19mm 1/2.8"↔1/3"↔1/2"↔1/1.8" image sensor [freestyle]

    • Mini — 20x20mm 1/3" image sensor [macroquad/X-Class]

    • Board — 40x40mm 1/3" image sensor [The year isn't 2010, what are you doing!]

      • Little known fact that above 650TVL introduces latency according to TBS zerozero product description. This was advertised to be faster than 1ms.

      The fastest CMOS camera ever is the fabled Caddx Turbo EOS2 v1, who is next to take the crown @ 1.5ms response time?

      Cameras with larger 1/2 sensors captures low light better than 1/3 sensors at the cost of slower response times (+/- 20ms).

      I think the reason is the on-board camera processor must work harder to export the frames from the sensor therefore a delay as a result. Denser television lines take longer since there are increased analog fields to work with.

      What is a fresnel zone?

      Imagine a oblong bubble between a wireless transmitter & receiver, this is the fresnel zone. Maintaining "good line of sight" with the antennas equals good fresnel zone as the area remains clear of obstructions/interference. The further away you are, the trickier to track the bubble all else being equal. Always point the antenna beam at the aircraft. Even part of the fresnel zone disrupted causes massive signal degradation. Do not violate the fresnel zone!

      What is a antenna tracker?

      This device mounted on a sturdy tripod triangulates GPS coordinates from R/C telemetry & moves the antenna to keep the fresnel zone coverage for you! Overkill for daily use.

      What are harmonics?

      These are frequencies generated at exact, whole-number multiples of a transmitted intended nominal frequency. Harmonics can only spread upward from the source transmission. Interference from harmonics are called spurious transmissions.

      What are nulls?

      Null direction is the direction where the signal is weakest. Desired direction is where the radiated RF signal is strongest. Always avoid Null direction pointing toward the craft/radio whenever possible. With diversity, one antenna can cover the other antenna's null direction.

      What dBm Sensitivity Means:

      Decibels relative to a milliwatt (dBm) is a logarithmic unit measuring power, where 0 dBm is 1 milliwatt (mW).

      Negative dBm values indicate power less than 1 mW (e.g., -30 dBm is 0.001 mW or 1 microwatt).

      Receiver Capability:

      A receiver's sensitivity is the minimum input signal strength it needs to accurately decode data, often measured at a specific bit error rate (BER).

      The Scale:

      Values closer to zero (less negative) are stronger signals; values further from zero (more negative) are weaker signals.

      Interpreting dBm Sensitivity Values: Better Sensitivity (More Negative): A capable receiver with -96 dBm sensitivity can go twice as far as a -90 dBm because it can detect weaker signals.

      Why It Matters:

      Range: Higher sensitivity (more negative dBm) allows for longer communication distances. Interference Immunity: A sensitive receiver can distinguish weak desired signals from background noise, less breakup, improving reliability. System Design: Balancing transmit power & receiver sensitivity is key for effective FPV.

      What is gain?

      The gain of an antenna is simply the measure of power of an antenna or video transmitter, measured in decibels, the formal definition is: The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit of measurement that expresses the magnitude of a physical quantity (typically power or intensity) relative to a specified or implied reference level. Antennas that you can buy will usually have a dB specification. This value gives you an idea of how the antenna will alter the radiation pattern. A perfectly isotropic antenna with 0 dB gain will have a radiation pattern that’s a perfect sphere from the antenna. As you increase gain you will alter the shape of this circle pattern to squash or squeeze it to get extra range in a particular axis. The desired directional patterns are determined by both amplitude & phase of the radiated energy.

      However in real life that is usually not possible so antennas such as "duck" antennas which have a gain of about 2.2dB will squad the pattern down a bit to gain extra horizontal range.

      As we increase gain even higher with directional antennas not only is the pattern squashed vertically, but also stretched in a particular direction horizontally to get a stronger beam in that direction. Strong gain means focused directive. When the ground is involved? Strong gain means more scattered! The net quality of a ground reflection depends on the topography of the surface. When the irregularities of the surface are much smaller than the wavelength, the dominant regime is that of specular reflection, & the receiver sees both the real antenna & an image of the antenna under the ground due to opposite polarity reflection. But if the ground has irregularities large compared to the wavelength, reflections will be scattered but shifted by random phases. This almost always happens at challenging terrains we fly in & high gain makes this way pronounced. With shorter wavelengths (ex. 5.8gHz frequencies), this is generally the case. This is why you see most obnoxious 13+dB antennas mounted on a tripod standing tall from the ground. So by increasing gain, the antenna (directional antenna) essentially stretches the radiation pattern out to form further in a specific direction to get extra distance. Typically onboard your aircraft you will always use an Omni directional antenna since it is constantly rotating but you can use a directional antenna on the ground that will need to always point at your aircraft to get extra range. Some of the larger military "drones" also use directional antennas onboard the aircraft mounted onto a pan-tilt module which will make them face the ground station (or satellite) to get extreme range! 4x video-transmitter output power = ~200% range @ +6dB. (all else being equal)

      What is Radiation Efficiency?

      How much the antenna "hears" without backfeed to the source. (Mitigates damage)

      What is multipathing?

      This is when the video transmission bounces several times before reaching the receiver. Each bounce makes the polarization be inverse & distortion occurs i.e. multipath. Multipath fading occurs when reflected signal is hitting the source @ 180º out of phase.

      What is a balun?

      A device that connects the balanced & unbalanced elements of a antenna.

      What is impedance?

      The opposition to alternating current presented by the combined effect of resistance & reactance in a circuit.

      This is important because the antenna mating connector must precisely match the 50Ω load on video transmitters.

      Side note: CVBS broadcast use 75Ω impedance.

      What is SWR?

      Voltage Standing Wave Ratio is the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on a transmission line measured across a frequency threshold. The closer to the 1:1 50Ω dummy load value the better. >1.6 SWR is bad.

      The lowest I've seen advertised is 1.1 SWR.

      What is axial ratio?

      This measures how circular a circularly polarized antenna's wave is. A large number is elliptical. Wave Polarization: Linear, Circular, and Elliptical

      What is Polarization?

      In transmitting antennas, polarization refers to the orientation of the electromagnetic (EM) fields produced by the antenna as energy radiates away from it. Specifically, polarization is defined by the direction of the electric field (E-field) component of the electromagnetic wave. This orientation determines the plane in which energy propagates & how it can be received by another antenna. Transmitting & receiving antennas are designed with a specific polarization as an intrinsic characteristic. For maximum signal transfer, both antennas must share the same polarization orientation. If they are misaligned, signal degradation occurs due to polarization mismatch losses. For example, a slant polarized transmitting antenna will radiate energy with its electric field aligned @ 45º. A receiving antenna must also be slant polarized to efficiently capture that energy.

      In FPV quadcopter systems, antenna polarization is one of the most critical yet frequently misunderstood aspects of RF signal transmission. Whether you’re a racing pilot needing reliable video through tight courses or a long-range enthusiast pushing distance limits, understanding polarization which Alex Greve & collaborators is credited to have introduced to the hobbyist world – particularly circular polarization – can mean the difference between crystal-clear video & frustrating signal breakup.

      Polarization basics & beyond

      Linear vs Circular Polarization

      All radio waves have polarization – the orientation of their electric field oscillation:

      Linear Polarization:

      Electric field oscillates in a single plane (vertical or horizontal)
      Examples: Dipole/Whip antennas, Moxon & Yagi antennas
      Advantages: Simple design, good for control links
      Disadvantages: Sensitive to antenna orientation changes
       Most important to match alignment with Linear as this is most sensitive to be out of phase. Vertical must be vertical & vice versa.

      Circular Polarization:

      Electric field rotates as the wave propagates
      Examples: Patch, Crosshair, Cloverleaf
      RHCP (Right Hand Circular Polarization): Clockwise rotation
      LHCP (Left Hand Circular Polarization): Counter Clockwise rotation
      Advantages: Maintains signal integrity during across majority of angles
      Disadvantages: Unless housing is ultrasonically sealed; are fragile

      Why FPV Systems Favor Circular Polarization

      A circularly-polarized wave may quite properly be considered as made up of a vertically-polarized wave imposed on a horizontally- polarized wave with both waves traveling in the same direction. At any chosen point, the fields of the two waves are in time quadrature with one another. FPV video systems overwhelmingly use circular polarization because:
      Orientation Independence: Remote Control aircraft constantly change attitude – circular polarization maintains signal regardless of roll/pitch/yaw
      Multipath Rejection: Naturally filters out reflected signals (more on this later)
      Interference Reduction: Allows multiple pilots to fly simultaneously with less crosstalk
      Why avoiding crosstalk is crucial because this is able to seperate the neighbouring frequencies having the same polarized wave forms.

      RHCP vs LHCP: Key Differences

      There’s no performance difference between RHCP & LHCP when used correctly. Unless you're talking about search engine results.

      While RHCP & LHCP are functionally identical in performance, their opposite rotation has important implications:

      Characteristic RHCP LHCP
      Rotation Direction Clockwise Counter-Clockwise
      Common Applications Standard FPV, GPS Alternate channel systems
      After Reflection Becomes LHCP Becomes RHCP
      Compatibility Must match RX/TX Must match RX/TX

      Mandatory Rule: Your video transmitter & receiver must use the same polarization type (both RHCP or both LHCP) for optimal performance. Up to -28dBm loss can be achieved with mismatched hand rotation.

      Parabolic Dishes focuses the radiation from a wave guide by reflecting it from a parabolic surface; the strong emerging waves should be straight as a result. In reality, lack of side lobes to stabilize the narrow beam-width makes this arduous to aim. This requires continuous, two-axis tracking to follow the aircraft accurately & takes a long time to setup arriving to a hillside.

      Follow these simple rules, even if rumors on the internet suggest otherwise, & you will have success in FPV.

      Airframe Preparation

      Start with the bare essentials & add equipment one step at a time, after each new equipment was added to proper range & stress tests. Including being @ 25mW on maiden flight/new environment.

      You will learn the limits of your system much closer. If something bad happens, is going to be within walking distance. That's good!

      Do not fly with a video system that is capable of outperforming your R/C system in terms of range.

      The chances to crash from a failsafe is larger than loss of video. The weakest link must not be your radio!

      Monitor the vitals of your airborne vehicle (R/C link & battery). Flying with a digital R/C link without Received Signal Strength Indicator is dangerous.

      With telemetry that comes with RSSI built-in everything, please make the most of your hardware!

      Do not fly at the limits of video, if you see noise in your picture, turn around & buy a stronger-gain receiver antenna before going out further.

      Minimizing Interference

      Stand up while piloting.

      This maintains the fresnel zone (as explained above) & ensures you aren't slouching being comfortable seated.

      Connectors have limited mating cycles, so remove only when necessary.

      Do not use 2.4GHz R/C unless you fly well within its range limits, in noise-free environments & always within LOS. Since this is most likely never the case, it is recommended to not use 2.4GHz R/C systems for longer range FPV. (further than 20km) 868mHz/915mHz R/C links can penetrate farther than 2.4Ghz pre-LoRa R/C systems.

      Note: recently obsolete with dual-band R/C links such as Jeti Duplex, Frsky Tandem & ELRS Xrossband.

      ExpressLongRangeSystem 2.4gHz is the last R/C link you'll ever need! Beating ImmersionRC EZ UHF, Dragonlink V3, Frsky R9M, OpenLRS distances while using a smaller wavelength! Fine tuning the modulation + packet rate is a pleasure to use.

      Figure 6-3: Sensitivity Performance of the Transceiver Modems

      Do not fly with a R/C frequency higher than the video frequency(e.g. 2.4GHz R/C, 900MHz video).

      Back in the archaic days of FPV, powerful video transmitters were paired with weak >100mW PPM/SBUS based R/C unlike the modern 250+mW LoRa based R/C systems today. What we have now will lap circles around those on any day of the week, twice on Sunday! A less extreme example is 1.2/1.3GHz video & 2.4GHz R/C isn't necessarily that the second harmonic from the video is stronger than the R/C link. Even though it falls within 100MHz offset from the 2.4GHz band. The issue is that the raised noise floor increases the potential of a failsafe|brownout.

      What will happen is that the spurious video transmitter will disturb the R/C link making your model fly away whilst unable to disarm. Video harmonic noise does swamp R/C receivers, be careful.

      When using powerful R/C transmitters, make sure your groundstation equipment is properly shielded.

      Why a RF shield is necessary is to protect the video receiver when in close proximity. A interference effect called front end overload occurs. When a powerful radio frequency (RF) signal smashes a receiver's input stage & exceeds the linear operating limits. Causes distortion, desensitization, and/or permanent hardware damage. Your R/C radio blasting one watt will overpower the video receiver's front-end amplifier, blinding it to the video signal. You have the potential to fry your precious receiver.

      Adding Return-To-Home (RTH) to an unreliable system does not increase the chances of getting your plane back. Work on making your system reliable without RTH first, then add RTH as an additional safety measure if you must. However a GPS to log coordinates in missions is mandatory.

      Sometimes you're lazy to fix a problem, I get it.

      Avoid powering the VTx directly from battery, step-up or step-down the voltage & provide a constant level of power to your VTx. Make sure your VTx runs until your battery dies.

      How will you know which way is up when going blind?

      Do not power your camera directly unless it works along the complete voltage range of your battery. Step-up or step-down the voltage & provide a constant level of power to your camera. Make sure your camera runs until your battery dies.

      A single battery system is safer than using two dedicated batteries for R/C & FPV. Two batteries in parallel even further mitigate sources of failure. Redundancy!

      When flying with R/C buddies that fly on 2.4GHz, or when flying in cities, it is perfectly possible to use 2.4GHz video provided you stick to the channels that do not lie in their band i.e. outside 2400-2480mHz.

      Friends don't let friends stomp on mutual channels.

      For wide video channels & “law compatibility”, use 5.8GHz video as explained here.

      Do not use diversity video receivers as a replacement for pointing your antennas, diversity should be used to mitigate polarization/multi-pathing issues.

      Improving the antenna gain on the receiver end is better than increasing the output power (except in RF-noisy areas). More tx power causes more issues with RF on your aircraft. 600mW is plenty of power!

      Try to achieve as much separation of the VTx & R/C receiver as possible to lower the RF noise floor & EMI interference.

      Shielded wires alternating current or twisted direct current cables only, anything else picks up RF noise causing problems. Twisting alternating current wires introduces crosstalk since the polarity passes both directions. This helps to the aircraft the best condition it can be!

      Do not buy the cheapest equipment unless it is proven to work reliably (e.g. parts falling off, multitudes of bug fix firmware updates, community hacks & mods are a good indicator of poor quality & something you do NOT want to buy for a safe system). Do due diligence & some research before sending your aircraft skyward!

      AKK & some boscam TS832 copies have noisy amplifiers making hazy video & must have a custom define "hotfix" in flight controller firmwares.

      Color Shifting, Horizontal tearing, Noise bands, Antenna Shadows/Fades & Spontaneous breakup is normal. This is not like cable TV.

      Culprits are the first results on a search engine. Why I wouldn't do this since it is better to blame yourself for the hardware failure & learn from the session. Rather than pointing the finger at manufacturers.

      Long Story Short

      Most important antennas are nearest to the ground because the earth's surface affects the signal. I admit I don't know why exactly. The easiest antenna to start with would be a cloverleaf antenna on your receiver & a skew planar antenna on your video transmitter because you are in the dark about this.

      Let's change that!

      Some FPV kits already include these antennas, but if not most vendors sell them as a pair of FPV antennas. These are Omni directional, circular polarized antennas which work well for FPV.

      A perfect omni directional beam looks like a sphere, however because of the vertical nulls — the result is closer to a torus shape.

      Pagoda & "Lollipop" antenna starts to widen the nulls of the torus into a umbrella like profile & will be desirable for receiving only.

      There are also antennas called double axii or dual hammers that are Phased array antennas use specific engineered antenna position (& impedance matched pcb magic) to make normal antennas constructively interfere to increase gain. In the case of the dual hammer or double axii, the radiation gain over the single element version is essentially doubled, but it comes at a 2D orthogonal slice profile resembling a pizza cutter.

      Generally price gives a good indication on the quality & precision of the antenna. When comparing the same type of antenna from different manufactures, the expensive one will usually have better range. This is because they are made using better materials, & with further precision.

      Think about whether you pilot the aircraft in front of yourself or behind you.

      However, that is not always the case & it’s up to you if you think it is worth to pay double to get a ~10% increase in range. As you become familiar with FPV flying & you desire further range you can upgrade to more directional systems such as a helical antenna.

      Excellent analog video has long-forgotten rules & therefore seen as the inferior option. I am passing the torch of knowledge onto you!

      Why analog in one sentence? This is the least restrictive & most predictable system you can own!

      Antenna gain matters! or "watch the avalanche grow."
